I think it comes down to whether or not time is spent on reinventing the wheel or pushing things forward. One could argue that with fewer distros, the time spent on maintaining packages could be used for other things, like hardware support, and that would be a good thing. Still, I believe that this way of thinking isn't entirely true to how open source software is developed. There isn't a certain amount of dev hours to allocate where needed, but rather people just doing what they like. You can't tell people "ok, we have enough tiling wms as it is now, you people start working on nouveau optimus support instead." It's possible that having fewer similar projects wouldn't mean significantly more work done on other things. Also, (imho) the whole point of having free software is to be able to modify it for your needs, so I think it's a good sign that people are doing just that. Someone might want a small distro to put on a usb stick, someone might want a full desktop with all the bells and whistles, and someone might want a server distro with commercial support. Personally, I think it would be good to for example have more open drivers, but I don't think it should be a goal in itself for GNU/Linux to gain market share. Let people use what works for them. The "marketplace of distros" ensure that we can vote with our feet if we don't like where a project is heading.
